links.note: In 1438 the pope confirmed a letter from William of Casale, head of the whole order. It made one of his friars, Bernardino of Siena, vicar of the order's houses in Italy set up 'under the holy name of observance'. The historian Henry Charles Lea traced these strict houses to 1368. That year the head of the order asked for a hermitage at Brugliano for Paoluccio Trinci and his men.

prose_changes.old: When Pope John XXII ordered the strictest Franciscans to give up their insistence on absolute poverty, four who refused were burned at Marseille in 1318, and in 1323 he declared it heretical to believe Christ and the apostles had owned nothing at all. Those who still would not submit, called fraticelli, survived for another century and a half in scattered communities across Italy and Provence, supported by lay sympathizers such as the beguins of Languedoc, who venerated the burned friars as martyrs and were hunted for it in turn. A trial at Rome in the 1460s finally ended them.
prose_changes.new: Pope John XXII ordered the strictest Franciscans to give up their stand on absolute poverty. Four who refused were burned at Marseille in 1318. In 1323 he declared it heretical to insist that Christ and the apostles had owned nothing at all. Those who still would not submit were called fraticelli. They lasted another century and a half in scattered communities across Italy and Provence. Lay friends kept them going, among them the beguins of Languedoc, who honored the burned friars as martyrs and were hunted for it in turn. After a public penance at Rome in 1467, they fade from sight.
prose_changes.reason: As in the long description: 'a trial at Rome in the 1460s finally ended them' becomes the 1467 penance Lea describes (lines 8493-8497); 'to believe' becomes 'to insist'. Long sentences split.

prose_changes.old: No community survived and no church descends from them. What survived was the argument. The poverty controversy forced both sides into working out theories of ownership, use and right that fed directly into later Western thinking about property, and the friars who fled the papal court over it — William of Ockham among them — turned the quarrel into political philosophy. It also left the beguins of Languedoc, remembered now almost entirely through the interrogations that destroyed them, and it left the poverty question itself, which kept returning inside the Franciscan family every time it reformed.
prose_changes.new: No community survived and no church descends from them. What survived was the argument. The poverty quarrel pushed both sides to work out what it means to own a thing, to use it, and to have a right to it. The friars who fled the papal court over it, William of Ockham among them, turned the quarrel into political thought. It also left the beguins of Languedoc, known now almost wholly through the questioning that destroyed them. And it left the poverty question itself. That question kept coming back inside the Franciscan family each time it reformed.
prose_changes.reason: 'Fed directly into later Western thinking about property' names no party and has no vendored or repo-cited source; removed. Ockham's political writings against John XXII are vendored (Scholz 1914), so that clause stays. Long sentence split.

prose_changes.old: This is a continuous institution: the same church, reorganized by the Council of Trent a generation later, is the Roman Catholic Church of today. Its material legacy from these centuries is unmissable — the papal palace at Avignon, the Vatican Library, the Sistine Chapel, the basilica of St Peter's begun in 1506. Its constitutional legacy is quieter and longer-running. The conciliar claim that a general council can judge a pope was defeated but never quite died, resurfacing in Gallicanism, in later Catholic reform movements, and in the arguments around the First Vatican Council four and a half centuries afterward. And the reforms that the fifteenth century's councils repeatedly voted and failed to enforce were still outstanding when Luther wrote.
prose_changes.new: This is a continuous institution. The same church, reorganized by the Council of Trent a generation later, is the Roman Catholic Church of today. Its material legacy from these centuries is hard to miss: the papal palace at Avignon, the Vatican Library, the Sistine Chapel, and St Peter's, begun in 1506. Its legacy in church law is quieter and has lasted longer. The claim that a general council can judge a pope was beaten but never quite died. In 1682 the French clergy appealed to the rulings of Constance in their Gallican Articles. In 1870 the First Vatican Council turned the claim down once more. And the reforms the councils of the 1400s kept voting for, and failed to enforce, were still waiting when Luther wrote.
